analytic.title: Monitoring of Workload Arrival Functions for Mixed-Criticality Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Integrating applications with different safety requirements on a common platform requires either certification of all applications to the highest safety level or "sufficient independence" among them. As the former typically is too costly, isolation mechanisms, such as monitoring, are key in the design of mixed-criticality systems.

We regard monitoring of activation patterns of real-time applications in mixed-criticality systems. Existing solutions monitor single tasks in isolation. We present a monitoring scheme which allows to monitor groups of tasks jointly. It allows to express correlations between activations and provides improved resource utilization as no isolation between tasks in a group is enforced.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The performance increase of processors for embedded systems makes integration of more functionality on a common platform ever more attractive. Yet, when applications have different requirements on safety, either they all have to be certified to the highest safety level, which is usually too expensive, or must show "sufficient independence" between applications of different safety-criticality [1]. In this paper we regard monitoring of timing properties to provide sufficient temporal independence.

Design processes for safety-critical real-time systems often employ formal model-based verification algorithms to prove adherence to constraints (e.g. [2], [3]). These analyses rely on the correctness of the input data, as e.g. task activation patterns. A common modelling for activation patterns is given through event arrival functions [2], [3], which give an upper bound on the number of activations that can be seen in any time interval of size Δt. For low-criticality tasks, for which the confidence in the input data may be low, these parameters have to be enforced in the system to ensure the given guarantees. This can be achieved through monitoring.

Existing methods to monitor and enforce task activation patterns [4], [5], [6], [7] that are modelled through event arrival functions work on tasks in isolation, i.e. each task has a separate monitor which regards only the activations of that single task. This enforces the behavior of each monitored task, i.e. whenever a task exceeds its activation budget, its activations are being blocked. However, the "independence" requirements for mixed-critical systems are less strict. It is only required that the interference from all lower criticality levels on a higher criticality level has to be bounded. In other words, the total interference from all low-critical tasks combined on a highcriticality task has to be bounded. This requirement is less strict because one low-criticality may exceed its budget on the cost of another low-criticality task. This case becomes especially relevant when the typical activation behavior of a task significantly deviates from the worst-case behavior, which is captured in the arrival function (e.g. for sporadic activations with minimum inter-arrival time or for correlations between task activations).
In this paper, we show how this relaxed independence requirement can be exploited in monitoring to consider activation correlations and to increase overall system utilization.
The key contributions are

• the application of the modelling for variable worst-case execution times of [8] to express the cumulative worstcase workload of a group of tasks, which is specified through a workload arrival function (WAF). • a constant overhead monitoring scheme, which enforces a given WAF, for a group of tasks. The response time analysis considering WAFs is out of the scope of this paper. An approach for this was presented in [8].

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. In Sec. II we review related work concerning modelling of event correlations and monitoring of timing properties. Then, we introduce our monitoring setup for enforcing the interference through groups of tasks (Sec. III) and the assumed system model (Sec. IV). In the main part in Sec. V we introduce our constant overhead monitoring scheme, and in Sec. VI we outline how the necessary configuration can be obtained from tests. In Sec. VII we provide an overhead evaluation of an actual software implementation. Finally, we evaluate the monitoring (Sec. VIII) and conclude (Sec. IX).

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: In this paper we provide an efficient mechanism to establish "sufficient temporal independence" in mixed-criticality realtime systems. Mixed-criticality systems have been studied in the domain of schedulability and response time analysis (e.g. [9], [10]). These approaches determine the schedulability of a system, in which tasks are attributed with multiple specifications (on worst-case execution times), depending on the certification level. The analysis assumes that task activations are revoked or delayed whenever the specified bounds of a given criticality level are exceeded. The detection of a specification exceedance is not addressed. The work of this paper can therefore be seen as complementary to those approaches because we provide exactly such a detection mechanism.
In the remainder of this section we review related work concerning (1) the modelling of groups of tasks and task correlations and (2) the monitoring of task activations.

In response time analysis the grouping of tasks and the consideration of correlations has shown to significantly improve analysis results also for realistic setups [11]. Grouping of tasks is used for hierarchical event models [12], [13], [14], which is mainly applied in the analysis of frame packing, where different messages are jointly transmitted in one communication frame. This does not translate into our monitoring setup because packed messages are serviced by the resource as one instance, i.e. one frame. We rather aim to enforce a maximum interference of several separate tasks.

Correlations between the activation of different tasks (intertask correlations) can be expressed through offsets [15], [16], [17]. However, the definition of offsets is only meaningful for periodic activation patterns. Thus, they cannot be used for sporadic activations, which are especially relevant for low-criticality applications (e.g. user interface). [8] introduced typed events and workload arrival functions (WAFs) to model correlations between activations of one task (intra-task correlations). Similar to demand bound functions [18] but without the notion of task deadlines, WAFs specify the worst-case workload that can be requested by a task in any time interval of size Δt. In this paper we build on this modelling of [8] and apply it to groups of tasks.

Monitoring real-time properties in safety-critical systems is common industrial practice; e.g. the automotive OSEK operating system standard provides for deadline monitoring facilities [19], [20], and the AUTOSAR timing protection [21] allows to monitor execution time, inter-arrival rates and blocking times of software components [22]. Common mechanisms to perform deadline and execution time monitoring are through watchdog timers -either in hardware or in software [23].

Monitoring task activations has been presented mainly based on event arrival functions (or the dual representation of minimum distance functions) [4], [5], [6], [7]. These monitoring schemes do not consider groups of tasks, and thus neither can reflect correlations between activations nor support bounding interference through groups rather than individual tasks. [24] presented a monitoring scheme that is based on demand bound functions and thus has a notion of workload. However, the runtime complexity is significant and the methodology is limited to EDF-scheduled systems.

An alternative to monitoring, which is however related, is the use of servers [25] (e.g. Constant-Bandwidth Servers [26], [27] or Latency-Rate Servers [28]). Server-based approaches assign a certain execution or invocation budget to a task. The execution/invocation of the task is monitored, and this way the budget is consumed. The budget is replenished according to the server strategy. This allows to control the amount of computation time a task receives. However, it usually requires a specific scheduling policy.

In this paper we aim to overcome these limitations and consider groups of tasks in monitoring. We monitor the worstcase requested workload of groups of tasks, which allows to bound the interference that they impose on other tasks.

div.head: III. MONITORING SETUP
div.p: In this section we introduce the monitoring setup, which we propose to bound the interference of a group of low-criticality tasks on high-criticality tasks. To illustrate this setup, we first describe the state-of-the-art event-based monitoring, and then we introduce the monitoring setup for worst-case workload monitoring of groups of tasks.

Assume a mixed-criticality system as depicted in Fig. 1a. On a processor two low criticality tasks τ lc-1 , τ lc-2 and one high criticality task τ hc are executing. The high criticality task holds the lowest priority. The worst-case execution times (WCET) C i of all tasks are known. The enforcement of WCETs is out of the scope of this paper. The aim of the presented monitoring is to ensure that the influence of the low-criticality tasks on the high-criticality task is bounded by enforcing their activation patterns. The interference among the low criticality tasks, however, does not need to be guarded.

In order to enforce a maximum interference that the lower criticality tasks have on the high criticality one, current eventbased monitoring schemes (as e.g. [4], [6], [7]) monitor the activation patterns of each task individually, i.e. a monitor ensures that a task's activation sequence does not violate a given event arrival function ᾱi . Such a scheme also enforces the interference between the low-criticality tasks because one task may not exceed its budget at the cost of another task in the same group. Furthermore, as the monitoring is being done individually, no correlations between activations of τ lc-1 and τ lc-2 can be considered. As a result, the critical instant [29] has to be assumed in the response time analysis of τ hc . Thus, such a monitoring scheme provides isolation where it is not necessary, requires over-approximations in the worst-case response time analysis because correlations are neglected, and causes additional runtime overhead through use of multiple monitors.

We propose to monitor tasks in groups, as shown in Fig. 1b. The task activations of both lower criticality tasks are monitored in conjunction. This permits to enforce correlations between the activations of both tasks. However, both tasks may have different WCETs, and thus the monitor has to consider the workload that an event may entail in the worst-case. For this we propose to type events and to consider a different worst-case execution time depending on the type. Response time analysis for such typed events has been presented by [8]. The analysis is based on workload arrival functions α(Δt), which denote the maximum workload that may be requested in a time interval of size Δt. This WAF α(Δt) directly specifies the interference on lower priority tasks. If no correlation between tasks in the group exists, the WAF is identical to the interference for the critical instant, i.e. ᾱ1 (Δt) * C 1 +ᾱ 2 (Δt) * C 2 . In case correlations exist, the interference is lower, and thus tighter bounds can be given. The derivation of those tighter bounds is also described in [8].
Enforcement of such WAFs has not been presented. Thus, this maximum interference of a group of low-criticality tasks on a high-critical one is not enforced in the system.

We propose to use typed events to denote the different worst-case execution times of tasks in a group. Based on this model we present a novel constant overhead monitoring scheme, which monitors adherence to WAFs representing the worst-case workload that may be requested through a set of typed events, and thus directly enforce the worst-case interference on lower priority tasks.

div.head: IV. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: Before we introduce monitoring according to workload arrival curves, we introduce the system model used throughout this paper. This includes defining the notions of event traces, which describe specific activation sequences in a system, and WAFs, which provide an upper bound on allowed activation patterns under consideration of WCETs. In this context monitoring requires to check whether a given trace satisfies a WAF.

We assume a platform that is scheduled according to static priorities. On this platform a set of communicating tasks T = {τ 1 , . . . , τ r } is executed. Tasks are activated by event arrivals at their input and then execute for at most their respective worst-case execution time of C i .

In order to reason about interference from groups of tasks, we introduce a novel modelling based on typed events [8], which was originally used to model intra-task correlations. A set of tasks with successive scheduling priorities can be jointly considered as a group T group ⊂ T taking into account their activation correlations. In this case they are considered as one virtual task (compare Fig. 1b). The virtual task is activated upon arrival of an activating event of any task in the group (OR-activation [3]). To associate an event with the corresponding task in the group, events may be of different types resulting in different worst-case execution times C i at the virtual task. We assume that all worst-case execution times C i of a group can be expressed as multiple of a common minimal execution time C GCD , which can be found as the greatest common divisor (GCD) of the individual WCETs. In the monitoring scheme, which we present, it is also safe to overapproximate WCETs to obtain such a GCD.

In order to have a notion on the temporal occurrence of events and the worst-case workload they may entail, we define an event trace, which describes a specific sequence of event occurrences and the corresponding worst-case requested workload.
div.formula: Definition 1 (Trace) An event trace of n max events is a function σ : [1, n max ] → N + × N +(1)
div.p: where σ(n) = (t, C) denotes that the n-th event occurs at time t and entails processing time of C.

For notationally simplicity let σ t (n) return the time and σ C (n) the requested worst-case processing time (i.e. WCET) of the n-th event. This description of a trace accurately describes a specific activation sequence of a group of tasks. An example trace is shown in figure 2a where vertical arrows denote event occurrences. t i denotes the corresponding time instant and C i the worst-case execution time that is associated with the type of the event.

The total accumulated worst-case workload W (n, m), i.e. the processing time if each event in the trace would execute for its associated WCET C i , that is requested through a task group in the time interval from the occurrence of the n-th event until the occurrence of the m-th event (inclusive) is
div.formula: W (n, m) = m i=n σ C (i)(2)
div.p: In many systems task activations are not strictly deterministic because e.g. tasks are activated through external events. To determine timing guarantees despite such uncertainties, analyses (as e.g. RTC [2] or CPA [3]) use worst-case abstractions of possible traces as input. These are referred to as event models.
A common means to describe event models is given by event arrival functions ᾱ(Δt). They provide an upper bound on the number of events that can be seen in any time interval of size Δt [2], [3].

In the context of this paper we group several tasks into one virtual task, where different events may cause different WCETs. To account for these variable worst-case execution demands, we use workload arrival functions, which provide an upper bound on the workload that can be requested in any time interval of size Δt, or formally Definition 2 (Upper Workload Arrival Function) The upper workload arrival function α is an increasing function
where α(Δt) describes an upper bound on the workload W requested during any time interval of size Δt.

Note, that workload arrival functions differ from demand bound functions (DBF) [18] as they do not incorporate a notion of deadlines. An example of an upper workload arrival curve is given in figure 2b. It shows that e.g. the maximum workload that is requested within a time interval of Δt 2 will never exceed a value of W 2 . Such workload arrival functions are a generalization of event arrival functions. If all events can cause an identical worst-case execution time, both are related through
div.formula: α(Δt) = C * ᾱ(Δt)(4)
div.p: In general, when different types of events with differing WCETs exist, the transformation is more complex. For analytical derivation of these WAFs and their consideration in worst-case response time analysis refer to [8]. In this paper we present a scheme for monitoring according to this generalized model of WAFs, i.e. we ensure that the requested worstcase workload of a group of tasks does not exceed specified bounds. To do so, we will start by defining a condition, when a given trace satisfies a WAF. We show that the overhead of checking satisfaction grows linearly with the trace size as is the case for event-based monitoring [7]. Then we will present a methodology to limit the monitoring overhead (in terms of memory and computation time) to a constant.

div.head: V. MONITORING OF REQUESTED WORKLOAD
div.p: In this section we introduce the formalization of the proposed monitoring scheme. We give a definition of satisfaction, reduce the monitoring overhead to a constant, and show that even for limited overhead we can monitor certain infinite WAFs.

div.head: A. Satisfaction of Workload Arrival Curves
div.p: In order to reason about monitoring of requested workload, we need to relate traces and workload arrival functions. First, we define when a trace satisfies a WAF. This satisfaction condition shall ensure that no more workload is requested than a WAF permits. It forms the basis for our monitoring scheme.

div.head: Definition 3 (Satisfaction of α) An event trace σ satisfies an upper workload arrival function α if
div.formula: ∀t 1 ≤ t 2 ∈ N : α(t 2 -t 1 ) ≥ W (i 1 , i 2 ) = i2 i=i1 σ C (i) (5) with i 1 = min(i : σ t (i) ≥ t 1 ) i 2 = max(i : σ t (i) ≤ t 2 ) (6)
div.p: This definition requires that during no time interval t 2t 1 more workload W (i 1 , i 2 ) is requested in the trace than is allowed by the WAF α(t 2t 1 ).

This satisfaction condition bears the caveat that it needs to be checked for all possible time instants t 2 , t 1 . Naturally, this is not feasible for monitoring, which has to be performed during system runtime. Therefore, we prove next that we do not need to check (5) for arbitrary time instants t 1 , t 2 but that it is sufficient to check only for those time instants at which events arrived, i.e. for all timestamps in the trace σ t (i).

div.head: Lemma 1 An event trace σ satisfies an upper workload arrival function α if
div.formula: ∀n ≤ m ∈ [1, n max ] : α(σ t (m) -σ t (n)) ≥ W (n, m) = m i=n σ C (i)(7)

Lemma 1 states that we only require to check the satisfaction condition for the timestamps in the trace σ t (i). Furthermore, we can directly deduce a satisfaction condition for continuous monitoring, where a given trace that satisfies a WAF is extended by appending a new event.

Corollary 1 Let a trace σ of length n max -1 satisfy a workload arrival function. If the trace is continued by an additional event with index n max , then the continued trace also satisfies the workload arrival function if
div.formula: ∀n ∈ [1, n max ] : α(σ t (n max ) -σ t (n)) ≥ W (n, n max ) = nmax i=n σ C (i) (9)
div.p: Proof: Directly follows from lemma 1. As a result from corollary 1 we obtain that for a continued trace we only need to check new events for satisfaction.

Nonetheless, even for continued traces the number of conditions to check for determining satisfaction of a WAF still depends on the number of events in the trace. Thus, the monitoring overhead grows with trace length and thus with system uptime. In the following section, we provide a methodology to limit the interval to check to a constant for WAFs that are limited to a certain interval. In Sec. V-C we show that this implicitly monitors according to an infinite arrival curve.

In the following section we show that limited WAFs actually monitor their more restrictive sub-additive closure.

div.head: C. Implicit Monitoring of infinite arrival curves
div.p: In this section we employ the concept of the sub-additive closure, which is known from from Network Calculus [30], to show that monitoring according to a limited workload arrival function implicitly monitors an unlimited workload arrival function.
The definition of a sub-additive closure from [30] is based on the min-plus convolution ⊗ of an arrival function, which is defined as
div.formula: (α ⊗ α)(Δt) = min 0<Δt <Δt {α(Δt ) + α(Δt -Δt )} (22)
div.p: The sub-additive closure is then given as Definition 5 [30] The sub-additive closure of a function α is given as
div.formula: closure(α) = inf n≥0 {α (n) } (23
div.p: where α (n) denotes the function obtained by repeating (n -1) convolutions ⊗ of α with itself.

In the scope of this paper only a key property of the subadditive closure closure(α) of a WAF α is relevant. The sub-additive closure closure(α) of a function α yields the largest sub-additive function that is smaller than α [30]. An example is given in Fig. 3. The solid line denotes a workload arrival function α of limited length l, which is sub-additive in the interval [0, l]. The dotted line denotes the sub-additive closure of this function. In the interval [0, l] it is identical to α because α is sub-additive in this domain. Beyond l it continues sub-additively. Sub-additive closures are also called "good" arrival functions as they tightly bound a trace, i.e. without over-approximation. [30] has proven the following key property of the sub-additive closure that is relevant in our scope of monitoring.

Lemma 4 (Theorem 1.2.1 in [30]) It is equivalent whether a trace is constrained through any wide-sense increasing arrival function or through the corresponding sub-additive closure, i.e. σ satisfies α ⇔ σ satisfies closure(α) (24) From this lemma we can conclude that it is equivalent whether we monitor a limited workload arrival function or its subadditive closure. For the example in Fig. 3 this means if we monitor according to the solid line, which is possible at constant overhead as we have shown in Sec. V-B, we implicitly also enforce the behavior of the dotted line, i.e. we can monitor any sub-additive closure at constant overhead.
Since the arrival functions of many parametrized activation patterns (e.g. periodic, sporadic, periodic bursts) are subadditive closures, these functions also have high practical relevance.
From the lemmata derived thus far we can also derive a satisfaction condition for arbitrary workload arrival functions that are not limited to a bounded interval.
Theorem 1 Let a given trace σ of length n max -1 satisfy a limited workload arrival function α l . Then the continued trace σ of length n max satisfies any (unlimited) α with
div.formula: ∀Δt ∈ N : α(Δt) ≥ closure(α l )(Δt) (25) if ∀n ∈ [ň min , n max ] : α l (σ t (n max ) -σ t (n)) ≥ W (n, n max )(26)
div.p: Proof: As α(Δt) ≥ closure(α l )(Δt), any trace that satisfies closure(α l ) also satisfies α. From lemma 4 we know that any trace that satisfies α l also satisfies closure(α l ). From lemmata 1 and 3 we know that α l satisfies the continued trace. Thus, the theorem follows.

With Theorem 1 we know that we can conservatively enforce any unlimited WAF α with limited overhead by monitoring a limited WAF α l that satisfies (25). This monitoring is exact, i.e. it yields no false positives if α(Δt) = closure(α l )(Δt). Otherwise the monitor may report a violation according to closure(α l ) although the original function α is not yet violated.

div.head: VI. RECORDING MONITOR CONFIGURATIONS
div.p: In the previous section we have shown that any arbitrary WAF can be monitored conservatively according to a limited WAF at constant overhead. Analytical derivation of WAFs based on typed events has been presented in the work of [8]. However, the effort put into modelling of low-criticality applications is typically low, and low-criticality applications are often only tested for correct functionality. In this section we briefly outline how the WAF required for group monitoring can be obtained from tests.

Monitoring according to the proposed scheme requires to check Eq. 9 for the past Δn events (Lemma 2). We can also use this satisfaction condition to record a monitoring configuration from observed behavior. We start with a group monitor with an arbitrarily chosen Δn, i.e. the length of the maintained trace and WAF can be arbitrarily chosen by the designer, while the choice influences overhead and tightness of the monitoring scheme. All explicitly defined values α Δt of the limited length WAF of the monitor are initialized to 0. Next, the testing of the low-criticality applications is performed. During this test whenever Eq. 9 is violated, we adapt the corresponding value of α(Δt) such that the satisfaction condition is satisfied again. As a result the trace observed during testing satisfies the obtained WAF by definition. For the deployed system the monitor is statically configured with the obtained limited WAF. Thus, the monitor permits no behavior of the task group that behaves worse than the tested behavior.

div.head: VII. SOFTWARE IMPLEMENTATION
div.p: Above we have formally shown that monitoring workload arrival functions can be achieved at constant overhead. In this section we show how this can be implemented in software in an RTOS to provide temporal isolation between applications of different criticalities.

The pseudo-code in Alg. 1 has to be executed whenever a task in a monitored group receives a new activation. The algorithm requires the current system time as input. Furthermore, it requires two buffers of length Δn to store the last Δn timestamps and event types, i.e. WCETs C i associated with the event type. Let index 0 denote the most current event. Furthermore, an inverse representation of the limited workload arrival function α l is stored in the system. This inverse α -1 l yields the minimum time interval in which a workload of W may be requested, i.e.
div.formula: α -1 l (W ) = min {Δt : α(Δt) ≥ W } (27
div.p: As we assume that all worst-case execution times are multiples of C GCD , we only evaluate the function at such multiples. Furthermore, the maximum workload that may ever be requested by Δn events is given through Δn * C max . Thus, we can store α -1 l in an array of length Δn * C max /C GCD , where α -1 l [W/C GCD ] = Δt yields the minimal time interval in which a workload of W may be requested.

The algorithm is performed as follows. First, the trace buffer is right shifted to disregard outdated trace events, and the most current trace event is stored in the respective buffers (lines 1-3). Then the accumulated workload W and the current event index i (most recent) are initialized to zero. While we have not yet checked Δn events (line 6), we proceed checking satisfaction. The accumulated workload is incremented by the event of the current index n maxi (line 7), and we check whether the time interval between the most current event and the event n maxi violates the time bound specified in the inverse workload arrival function (line 8). If this is the case, an exception is triggered in the RTOS.

div.head: VIII. EVALUATION
div.p: In this section we evaluate the benefits of monitoring of groups of tasks vs. individual monitoring of single tasks. We investigate two different aspects: 1) the benefits of the laxer isolation compared to individual monitoring, which allows to reclaim slack between tasks in a group and 2) the reduced interference on lower priority tasks when correlations between activations of tasks in a group can be guaranteed through the proposed group monitoring. Both evaluations are based on a synthetic set of testcases that we have executed on the Cortex-M3 implementation.

div.head: A. Slack Reclamation
div.p: We evaluate the benefits through the laxer isolation of group monitoring compared to individual monitoring based on the number of exceptions that the respective monitoring scheme triggers. The proposed group monitoring allows a task to activate more frequently if another task in the same group does not exploit its total allowable number of activations completely. Thus, we expect to see fewer exceptions for group monitoring than for individual monitoring.

To investigate this, we have pseudo-randomly generated tasksets with a group of 2, 4, 8 and 16 sporadic tasks. The worst-case execution times were randomly assigned in an interval [1ms, 5ms] with increments of 1ms. The tasks were activated sporadically while the mean inter-arrival rate was chosen to achieve different utilizations.

For individual monitoring each task was monitored according to a randomly assigned minimum inter-arrival time of 5ms, 10ms, 15ms or 20ms, i.e. whenever a task is activated faster than at its minimum inter-arrival time, individual monitoring triggers an exception. The group monitoring was configured such that it does not encode any correlations, and thus it allows identical interference on lower priority tasks as individual monitoring, i.e. α(Δt) = i C i * ᾱi (Δt). Since arrival functions of the constituent sporadic tasks are subadditive closures, the monitoring is tight. An example of two event arrival functions and the corresponding workload arrival function that were used to configure the monitors is given in Fig. 4.

We executed each of the 320 testcase systems for 60 seconds on the microcontroller implementation and counted the number of exceptions of the respective monitoring schemes. Fig. 5a shows the relative number of exceptions, i.e. In these figures smaller values indicate a larger improvement through workload monitoring. In Fig. 5a we see that for low utilizations workload monitoring triggers 10% of the exceptions of individual monitoring. For larger utilizations the benefit decreases to ∼30%. Workload monitoring performs better for low utilizations because tasks leave more slack which can be used by other tasks in the group. Naturally, this effect decreases with increasing utilization. In Fig. 5b we see the relative number of exceptions over the number of tasks, i.e. the size of the monitored group. For small groups workload monitoring outperforms individual monitoring by a factor of ∼2. With increasing group size the advantage increases drastically because the probability that all tasks in the group are activated simultaneously diminishes. In fact, those systems that contained 16 tasks in the monitored group triggered no exceptions at all, while individual monitoring still caused a significant number of exceptions.

From this evaluation on slack reclamation we see that the relaxed isolation of group monitoring allows to admit a significantly higher number of low criticality task activations, while providing the same bounded interference on lower priority tasks. The effect is most prominent for a low utilization of the tasks in the group and for large group sizes.

div.head: B. Interference Reduction
div.p: Next, we evaluate the interference on lower priority tasks that can be guaranteed with group monitoring when task activations of the monitored group are correlated.

When task activations are correlated, their combined interference on lower priority tasks can be more accurately described with workload arrival curves then with event arrival curves. This is because in general α(Δt) ≤ i C i * ᾱi (Δt) holds. This tighter bound on the interference can be enforced with the proposed group monitor but cannot be enforced with individual monitors, as e.g. [5], [6], [7].

To investigate the influence of correlations on enforceable interference, we use the synthetic tasksets with 4 tasks in a group and activate each task with its minimum inter-arrival time. However, we additionally enforce minimum distances between activations of different tasks in the group by delaying activations, thus generating correlations in the group. To parametrize the amount of correlations among the tasks, the minimum distance between any two successive activations of all tasks in the group is set to σ * C max = σ * 5ms, where σ is the parametrization value, i.e. for σ = 0 no correlation is enforced and the critical instant can occur. For any other value of σ, there is a minimal distance between any two activations.

We record the WAF for the entire group α group according to the scheme in Sec. VI. Furthermore, we record the event arrival functions for each task individually and calculate the interference that would be enforced through individual monitors, i.e. α ind. (Δt) = i C i * ᾱi (Δt). Thus, we obtain the tightest configuration for each monitoring scheme at which no exceptions w.r.t. the observed behavior are triggered. For the respective configuration we obtain the maximum interference that can be guaranteed to lower priority tasks, i.e. the respective WAF. In other words, given the monitors shall allow the observed behavior, the determined WAFs yield the worst-case interference on lower priority tasks.

We compare the mean relative enforced interference of both monitoring approaches over the length of a hyper-period (Δt ∈ [0ms, 60ms]), i.e. We see that without any correlations (i.e. σ = 0) group monitoring provides no benefits w.r.t. interference2 . This was expected because simultaneous activations of all tasks can actually occur when no correlations exist. However, when correlations between activations exist, the interference that is enforced through group monitoring is significantly lower, than that of individual monitoring. Furthermore the benefit increases with increasing correlation. In our experiments, the interference that is permitted by group monitoring decreased approximately linearly down to a value of ∼ 60% of that of individual monitoring for activation offsets equal to the largest WCET of the tasks in the group (i.e. σ = 100%).

The evaluation of the proposed monitoring scheme has shown the two major benefits of considering tasks in groups Fig. 6: Evaluation of Correlation for monitoring in mixed-criticality systems. 1) When tasks do not activate as often as allowed by the respective event model (e.g. for sporadic tasks), group monitoring yields a significantly lower number of exceptions (i.e. higher utilization) than individual monitoring while providing the same interference guarantees for lower priority tasks. 2) When activations of tasks in a group are correlated, this correlation can be exploited through group monitoring. This yields a lower worst-case interference that has to be considered in the analysis of lower priority tasks.

div.head: IX. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper we have proposed a monitoring scheme to enforce bounded interference between groups of tasks. We have shown how the modelling of typed events presented by [8] can be used to model the interference of groups of tasks through workload arrival functions. In our context, these functions denote the maximal workload that may be requested by a group of tasks in given time interval. We have formally derived a constant overhead (runtime and memory) monitoring scheme which allows to enforce such workload arrival functions in the system. We have shown that also in an actual implementation in an RTOS this constant overhead is in an acceptable range. In an evaluation based on synthetic testcases, which were executed on the RTOS implementation, we have shown how this monitoring scheme can increase the number of admitted activations compared to existing individual monitoring at identical maximum interference on lower priority tasks. Furthermore, we have shown that the enforced interference on lower priority tasks is significantly lower when correlations are encoded in the enforced workload arrival functions. This is not possible for individual monitoring.
